related_questions.question: What is the financial burden of pressure ulcers?
related_questions.snippet: We hear a lot about how much pressure ulcers cost the US economy. Padula and Delarmente (2019) estimated that government money spent on hospital-acquired pressure injury in 2016 exceeded $26.8 billion. About 59% of these costs were disproportionately attributable to a small rate of Stage 3 and 4 full-thickness wounds.

related_questions.question: What are the rates of hospital-acquired pressure injuries?
related_questions.snippet: The incidence of pressure injuries in hospitalized patients has been estimated at 5.4 per 10,000 patient-days, and the rate of hospital-acquired pressure injuries (HAPIs) has been estimated at 8.4% (Li et al., 2020). Over 50% of reported pressure injuries in hospitals were stage 2 or higher (Li et al., 2020).

text_blocks.snippet: Pressure injuries, also known as pressure ulcers or bedsores, significantly impact healthcare costs, both for individual patients and the healthcare system. Treatment can range from $20,900 to $151,700 per injury, with the total cost of pressure injuries in the US estimated to be between $9.1 and $11.6 billion annually. These costs are driven by factors like extended hospital stays, increased risk of infections, and the need for specialized wound care.

list.title: Individual Patient Care:
list.snippet: Treatment costs can vary widely depending on the severity of the injury, ranging from $20,900 to $151,700 per pressure ulcer, according to the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ).

list.title: Hospital Stays:
list.snippet: Each pressure injury can add an estimated $43,180 to a hospital stay.

list.title: Longer Hospital Stays:
list.snippet: Pressure injuries, particularly those in later stages (3 and 4), can lead to significantly longer hospital stays, often extending the stay by weeks, and potentially longer if complications arise.

list.title: Increased Risk of Infection:
list.snippet: Pressure injuries can create pathways for infection, including sepsis, cellulitis, and bone infections, further increasing treatment costs.

list.title: Specialized Wound Care:
list.snippet: Treatment may involve specialized dressings, debridement (removal of damaged tissue), and even surgical procedures, all contributing to higher costs.

list.title: National Costs:
list.snippet: The total annual cost of pressure injuries in the US is estimated to be between $9.1 and $11.6 billion.
Preventing pressure injuries is significantly more cost-effective than treating them.
Risk-stratified prevention, focusing on high-risk patients, can be a particularly cost-effective strategy.
Investing in pressure injury prevention programs: can lead to substantial cost savings for healthcare facilities and reduce the overall burden on the healthcare system.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, pressure injuries are a costly healthcare issue, both for individual patients and the healthcare system as a whole. However, investing in prevention strategies can significantly reduce these costs and improve patient outcomes.
